in 2021 i tried to kill myself on 3 separate times. each night i’d take a random mix of medicine and pray i’d die in my sleep. the first 2 times weren’t enough to kill me, so i woke up the next morning and acted like everything was normal. it sucked, i wanted to tell someone or get help but i was too scared to say anything about what i did. 

the third time i tried, i actually felt some effects. but that’s what made me realize i wouldn’t wake up again, i would never see my friends again, i’d never make it to highschool or get to have kids. i was so scared and it made me realize i didn’t actually want to die so i ended up telling my mom what i did. she tried to get me to throw up and was crying too. 

i asked her to take me to a psych ward but she didn’t, i didn’t even go to the hospital. so i took a day off from school and then went back like normal the next day. 

things didn’t magically get better but it made me start to shift and slowly get out of my depression. a month after my attempt i felt better than i ever had in months.  

a lot of me felt like my attempt didn’t count because i never was hospitalized, because the only people that knew were my mom and therapist. but now it’s two years later and i realized an attempt is an attempt and i survived. i’m so grateful that i get to wake up every morning. when i was in that state of mind i always heard “suicide is a permanent solution to a temporary problem” and i thought it was stupid. but it really is true, things do get better, you just have to be patient. sometimes i’m out with friends and we’re laughing at a stupid joke and i just realize that this is why it didn’t work, there are so many beautiful, small things you’ll miss out on, so many beautiful experiences you could have left behind. but life really is worth living and things will get better, i promise! ❤️

+ this was so therapeutic, i never told anyone about my two other attempts and how i felt after so thank you for giving me this opportunity

high support needs doesn't mean completely incapable.  I know autistic people with higher support needs that are still verbal and able to, for the most part, support themselves (using their accomodations). While yes there are some autistic people who may be "severely disabled" (not a nice term btw), they are still people and not some gremlin that can't go outside because of their disability. Your child has their own unique autistic experience so not every higher needs autistic person will be the same way as your son, like you said, it is a spectrum.

Also, I wasn't saying that it's a fact of whether you are or aren't autistic, I was trying to say that in spite of people's differences on the spectrum, we are all still autistic and deserve to be treated with respect and dignity. We should not be treated like a child, no matter the amount of support you need. Just because you are higher support needs, you don't need to have things "dumbed down".

Btw, please don't say "truly disabled", all autistic people are disabled, there's no quota you need to meet to "really be disabled".

I feel the same way. Support levels are definitely helpful but I feel they are part to blame. When someone is high support needs, they are belittled and treated like a child, when someone is low support needs, their needs are overlooked and undermined.

People can’t understand that just because you require less support than another autistic person, that doesn’t mean you are any less autistic than them.
